title: Cruelty as a divorce ground - what courts actually accept as evidence
p1:
Many people think cruelty in divorce means only physical violence.

But courts often look at a much wider picture — and some accepted forms of cruelty may surprise you.
p2: Cruelty can include repeated harmful behaviour that makes continuing the marriage unreasonable, such as serious harassment, constant humiliation, threats, or conduct that causes significant emotional suffering. A single argument or ordinary marital disagreement usually is not enough. Courts typically look for evidence showing a pattern, impact, and seriousness of the behaviour.
p3:
The evidence can matter as much as the allegation. Messages, emails, medical records, witness statements, financial records, and documented incidents may help establish what actually happened. The key insight: courts usually decide based on proof of the conduct and its effect, not simply on one person's claim.

Keeping records of important incidents can make facts clearer when disputes arise.
